issues.legal_issue: A mutual mistake about the area of land to be sold makes the sale agreement void when the area is essential to the agreement.
material_facts: The parties entered into a written agreement for the sale of agricultural land and paid earnest money.
The agreement and pleadings reflected uncertainty about whether the land area was measured in different units, and the parties understood the area differently.
The lower appellate court found that the parties were not ad idem about the land area and that the area was essential to the agreement; the High Court upheld that finding.
issues.conclusion: The agreement was void under Section 20 of the Contract Act because both parties were mistaken about an essential matter of fact.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(g), 2(h), 10, 13, 14 and 20 of the Contract Act require an agreement enforceable by law and founded on free consent; consent requires that the parties agree on the same thing in the same sense. Under Section 20, an agreement is void when both parties make a mistake about a fact essential to it. The area of the land was essential, particularly because the price was calculated by reference to that area; this was not merely an erroneous opinion about value. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A purchaser brought a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell land.
predicates.different_understandings_of_land_area: The seller and purchaser understood the land's stated measurement differently, resulting in different views of the area to be sold.
predicates.land_area_essential_to_sale: The area of the land was material to the transaction, including because the sale price depended on it.

issues.definition: When a purchaser seeks specific performance and the parties understood an essential land area differently, the sale agreement is void.

issues.legal_issue: A forfeiture term cannot be enforced when it is part of an agreement void for mutual mistake about an essential matter.
material_facts: The agreement provided that the earnest money would be forfeited if the purchaser failed to pay the balance and obtain the sale deed within the specified time.
The purchaser was found not to have been ready and willing to pay the full sale consideration.
The parties had different understandings about the land area, an essential matter, and the agreement was therefore void.
issues.conclusion: The seller could not enforce the forfeiture term or retain the earnest money under it because the term formed part of the void agreement.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 73 and 74 of the Contract Act concern remedies for breach of a valid and binding agreement. A forfeiture stipulation forming part of an agreement void under Section 20 cannot be enforced. The terms of a void agreement cannot generally be severed and enforced independently, unless a clause is a separate and severable agreement; no such exception applied here. No earlier case was relied on for this issue.

issues.legal_issue: An advance received under an agreement void from its inception for mutual mistake must be restored when the agreement is later discovered to be void.
material_facts: The purchaser paid earnest money to the seller under the sale agreement.
The agreement was void from its inception because both parties were mistaken about the essential area of land to be sold.
The parties' mistake and the agreement's invalidity were recognized after the agreement had been made, and the seller had received the benefit of the advance.
issues.conclusion: The seller was required to refund the earnest money, with interest as ordered by the lower appellate court.
issues.legal_principle: Section 65 of the Contract Act requires a person who has received an advantage under an agreement discovered to be void to restore it or compensate the person from whom it was received. The expression includes an agreement void from its inception when the parties discover the mistake later. The Court relied on Thakurain Harnath Kuar v. Thakur Indar Bahadur Singh, AIR 1922 PC 403, and Ram Chandra Misra v. Ganesh Chandra Gangopadhya, AIR 1917 Cal 786. The ruling was confined to an agreement discovered to be void under Section 20 for mutual mistake.
